claim: Desmosomes are adhesive junctions composed of two desmosomal cadherins: desmocollin (Dsc) and desmoglein (Dsg).
source: Desmosomes are adhesive junctions composed of two desmosomal cadherins: desmocollin (Dsc) and desmoglein (Dsg).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about desmosome composition.

claim: E-cadherin (Ecad) facilitates desmosome assembly via an unknown mechanism.
source: Previous studies demonstrate that E-cadherin (Ecad), an adhesive protein that interacts in both trans (between opposing cells) and cis (on the same cell surface) conformations, facilitates desmosome assembly via an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This claim references previous studies and identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: Ecad interacts with isoform 2 of Dsg via a conserved Leu-175 on the Ecad cis binding interface.
source: Using AFM force measurements, we demonstrate that Ecad interacts with isoform 2 of Dsg via a conserved Leu-175 on the Ecad cis binding interface.
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM force measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ecad is enriched in nascent desmosomes.
source: Super-resolution imaging reveals that Ecad is enriched in nascent desmosomes, supporting a role for Ecad in early desmosome assembly.
evidence: This claim is supported by super-resolution imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Desmosome assembly is initiated at sites of Ecad mediated adhesion.
source: Finally, confocal imaging demonstrates that desmosome assembly is initiated at sites of Ecad mediated adhesion, and that Ecad-L175 is required for efficient Dsg2 and desmoplakin recruitment to intercellular contacts.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ecad-L175 is required for efficient Dsg2 and desmoplakin recruitment to intercellular contacts.
source: Finally, confocal imaging demonstrates that desmosome assembly is initiated at sites of Ecad mediated adhesion, and that Ecad-L175 is required for efficient Dsg2 and desmoplakin recruitment to intercellular contacts.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ecad trans interactions at nascent cell-cell contacts initiate the recruitment of Dsg through direct cis interactions with Ecad which facilitates desmosome assembly.
source: We propose that Ecad trans interactions at nascent cell-cell contacts initiate the recruitment of Dsg through direct cis interactions with Ecad which facilitates desmosome assembly.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Classical cadherins mediate cell-cell adhesion in all soft tissue and play critical roles in tissue morphogenesis.
source: While classical cadherins mediate cell-cell adhesion in all soft tissue and play critical roles in tissue morphogenesis, desmosomal cadherins mediate robust cell-cell adhesion in tissues like the epidermis and heart that are exposed to significant levels of mechanical stress (Dusek et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dusek et al., 2007.

claim: Desmosomal cadherins mediate robust cell-cell adhesion in tissues like the epidermis and heart that are exposed to significant levels of mechanical stress.
source: While classical cadherins mediate cell-cell adhesion in all soft tissue and play critical roles in tissue morphogenesis, desmosomal cadherins mediate robust cell-cell adhesion in tissues like the epidermis and heart that are exposed to significant levels of mechanical stress (Dusek et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dusek et al., 2007.

claim: There are four Dsg isoforms (Dsg1-4) and three Dsc isoforms (Dsc1-3).
source: There are two types of desmosomal cadherins: desmoglein (Dsg) and desmocollin (Dsc), which are organized into four Dsg isoforms (Dsg1-4) and three Dsc isoforms (Dsc1-3) (Getsios et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Getsios et al., 2004.

claim: Dsg2 and Dsc2 are widely expressed in the epithelia and are also found in non-epithelial cells such as in the myocardium of the heart and lymph node follicles.
source: Of these isoforms, Dsg2 and Dsc2 are widely expressed in the epithelia and are also found in non-epithelial cells such as in the myocardium of the heart and lymph node follicles (Getsios et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Getsios et al., 2004.

claim: Loss of Dsg2 is embryonically lethal.
source: Loss of Dsg2 is embryonically lethal (Eshkind et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eshkind et al., 2002.

claim: Mutations in Dsg2 and Dsc2 cause arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC), a hereditary heart disease.
source: while mutations in Dsg2 (Awad et al., 2006) and Dsc2 (Syrris et al., 2006) cause arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC), a hereditary heart disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Awad et al., 2006 and Syrris et al., 2006.

claim: Isoforms 1 and 3 are restricted to complex epithelial tissues.
source: In contrast, isoforms 1 and 3 are restricted to complex epithelial tissues (Green and Simpson, 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Green and Simpson, 2007.

claim: Loss of function of isoforms 1 and 3 leads to epidermal fragility, such as in the autoimmune blistering disease pemphigus.
source: and their loss of function leads to epidermal fragility, such as in the autoimmune blistering disease pemphigus (Amagai and Stanley, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Amagai and Stanley, 2012.

claim: Ecad localizes to the intercellular region of the bovine tongue epithelial desmosomes.
source: Immuno-electron micrographs demonstrate that Ecad localizes to the intercellular region of the bovine tongue epithelial desmosomes (Jones, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jones, 1988.

claim: Blocking Ecad adhesion with antibodies delay desmosome formation in MDCK cells and in human keratinocytes.
source: Blocking Ecad adhesion with antibodies delay desmosome formation in MDCK cells (Gumbiner et al., 1988) and in human keratinocytes (Lewis et al., 1994; Wheelock and Jensen, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gumbiner et al., 1988, Lewis et al., 1994, and Wheelock and Jensen, 1992.

claim: Desmosome formation in keratinocytes requires junctional initiation by the classical cadherins, Ecad or P-cadherin (Pcad).
source: Desmosome formation in keratinocytes requires junctional initiation by the classical cadherins, Ecad or P-cadherin (Pcad) (Amagai et al., 1995; Michels et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Amagai et al., 1995 and Michels et al., 2009.

claim: Ecad and Pcad deficient mice show defective desmosome assembly.
source: Consequently, Ecad and Pcad deficient mice show defective desmosome assembly (Tinkle et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tinkle et al., 2008.

claim: Ecad interacts laterally to form cis dimers on the same cell surface.
source: Since Ecad interacts laterally to form cis dimers on the same cell surface (Harrison et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harrison et al., 2011.

claim: Ecad molecules from opposing cells interact in a trans strand-swap dimer conformation.
source: while Ecad molecules from opposing cells interact in a trans strand-swap dimer conformation (Boggon et al., 2002; Parisini et al., 2007; Vendome et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boggon et al., 2002, Parisini et al., 2007, and Vendome et al., 2011.

claim: Ecad molecules from opposing cells interact in a trans X-dimer conformation.
source: and a trans X-dimer conformation (Ciatto et al., 2010; Harrison et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ciatto et al., 2010 and Harrison et al., 2010.

claim: L175 mediates homophilic Ecad cis dimerization.
source: Previous structural studies have shown that L175 mediates homophilic Ecad cis dimerization (Harrison et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harrison et al., 2011.

claim: The interactions between Ecad and Dsg2 are short-lived.
source: The interactions between Ecad and Dsg2 are short-lived and as desmosomes mature, Dsg2 dissociates from Ecad and forms stable bonds with Dsc2 to mediate robust adhesion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript, particularly the dynamic force spectroscopy measurements.

claim: As desmosomes mature, Dsg2 dissociates from Ecad and forms stable bonds with Dsc2 to mediate robust adhesion.
source: The interactions between Ecad and Dsg2 are short-lived and as desmosomes mature, Dsg2 dissociates from Ecad and forms stable bonds with Dsc2 to mediate robust adhesion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript, particularly the dynamic force spectroscopy measurements and imaging data.

claim: The probability of homophilic Dsg2 interaction in either the presence (1.6 ± 0.3%) or absence (2.5 ± 0.4%) of Ca2+ was comparable to nonspecific adhesion (1.2 ± 0.2% in Ca2+ and 1.4 ± 0.2% in EGTA).
source: In agreement with our previous results (Lowndes et al., 2014), the probability of homophilic Dsg2 interaction in either the presence (1.6 ± 0.3%) or absence (2.5 ± 0.4%) of Ca2+ was comparable to nonspecific adhesion (1.2 ± 0.2% in Ca2+ and 1.4 ± 0.2% in EGTA).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM force measurements presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Dsc2/Dsc2 showed a Ca2+-dependent homophilic interaction, with a binding probability of 4.1 ± 0.5% in Ca2+ and 2.0 ± 0.3% in EGTA.
source: In contrast, Dsc2/Dsc2 showed a Ca2+-dependent homophilic interaction (Lowndes et al., 2014), with a binding probability of 4.1 ± 0.5% in Ca2+ and 2.0 ± 0.3% in EGTA (corresponding nonspecific binding was 1.6 ± 0.2% and 1.3 ± 0.2% in Ca2+ and EGTA, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM force measurements presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Heterophilic interactions between Dsc2 (on AFM tip) and Dsg2 (on CS) were Ca2+-independent, with binding probabilities of 4.8 ± 0.5% in Ca2+ and 5.6 ± 0.5% in EGTA.
source: Heterophilic interactions between Dsc2 (on AFM tip) and Dsg2 (on CS) were Ca2+-independent (Lowndes et al., 2014), with binding probabilities of 4.8 ± 0.5% in Ca2+ and 5.6 ± 0.5% in EGTA (nonspecific binding levels were 1.4 ± 0.1% and 1.3 ± 0.1% in Ca2+ and EGTA, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM force measurements presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Ecad showed a Ca2+-dependent homophilic interaction with a binding probability of 5.4 ± 0.7% in Ca2+ and 2.0 ± 0.3% in EGTA.
source: As expected, Ecad also showed a Ca2+-dependent homophilic interaction with a binding probability of 5.4 ± 0.7% in Ca2+ and 2.0 ± 0.3% in EGTA (corresponding nonspecific binding was 0.5 ± 0.1% in Ca2+ and 0.9 ± 0.3% in EGTA) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM force measurements presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Ca2+-independent heterophilic interactions between Dsg2 (on CS) and Ecad (on AFM tip) were measured with binding probabilities of 5.7 ± 0.5% and 8.4 ± 0.6% in the presence of Ca2+ and EGTA respectively.
source: Surprisingly, we also measured Ca2+-independent heterophilic interactions between Dsg2 (on CS) and Ecad (on AFM tip) with binding probabilities of 5.7 ± 0.5% and 8.4 ± 0.6% in the presence of Ca2+ and EGTA respectively (nonspecific binding: 0.9 ± 0.1% in Ca2+ and 1.1 ± 0.1% in EGTA).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM force measurements presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Dsc2 on AFM tip and Ecad on the CS did not show any heterophilic binding either in Ca2+ or in EGTA.
source: In contrast, Dsc2 on AFM tip and Ecad on the CS did not show any heterophilic binding either in Ca2+ or in EGTA; while a binding probability of 0.5 ± 0.2%, comparable to nonspecific adhesion of 1.1 ± 0.1%, was measured in Ca2+, the binding frequency of Dsc2/Ecad interactions in EGTA was 0.8 ± 0.2% similar to nonspecific binding of 1.1 ± 0.1%.
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM force measurements presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Dsg2 and Ecad form a Ca2+-independent heterophilic dimer while Dsc2 does not bind heterophilically to Ecad.
source: Our binding probability measurements thus demonstrate that Dsg2 and Ecad form a Ca2+-independent heterophilic dimer while Dsc2 does not bind heterophilically to Ecad.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the AFM force measurements presented in Figure 1E.

claim: The off-rate of Dsc2/Dsc2 dimers was 1.26 s−1.
source: This analysis showed that the off-rate of Dsc2/Dsc2 dimers (Figure 2A) and Dsg2/Ecad dimers (Figure 2C) were comparable with a k0off of 1.26 s−1 and 1.24 s−1 respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamic force spectroscopy measurements presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The off-rate of Dsg2/Ecad dimers was 1.24 s−1.
source: This analysis showed that the off-rate of Dsc2/Dsc2 dimers (Figure 2A) and Dsg2/Ecad dimers (Figure 2C) were comparable with a k0off of 1.26 s−1 and 1.24 s−1 respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamic force spectroscopy measurements presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The lifetime of the Dsc2/Dsg2 dimer was 6x longer than either the Dsc2/Dsc2 or the Dsg2/Ecad with a k0off of 0.20 s−1.
source: In contrast, the lifetime of the Dsc2/Dsg2 dimer (Figure 2B) was 6x longer with a smaller k0off of 0.20 s−1, demonstrating that the Dsg2/Dsc2 dimer was more stable than either the Dsc2/Dsc2 or the Dsg2/Ecad.
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamic force spectroscopy measurements presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The Dsg2/Dsc2 dimer was more stable than either the Dsc2/Dsc2 or the Dsg2/Ecad.
source: In contrast, the lifetime of the Dsc2/Dsg2 dimer (Figure 2B) was 6x longer with a smaller k0off of 0.20 s−1, demonstrating that the Dsg2/Dsc2 dimer was more stable than either the Dsc2/Dsc2 or the Dsg2/Ecad.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the dynamic force spectroscopy measurements presented in Figure 2.

claim: Upon dissociation of Dsg2/Ecad and Dsc2/Dsc2 complexes, the free Dsg2 and Dsc2 would preferentially bind.
source: These measurements suggest that, upon dissociation of Dsg2/Ecad and Dsc2/Dsc2 complexes, the free Dsg2 and Dsc2 would preferentially bind.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the dynamic force spectroscopy measurements.

claim: Recent solution binding affinity measurements of desmosomal cadherins have shown heterophilic interactions are stronger than homophilic binding.
source: In agreement with our data, recent solution binding affinity measurements of desmosomal cadherins have shown heterophilic interactions are stronger than homophilic binding (Harrison et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harrison et al., 2016.

claim: Ecad levels were enriched in nascent desmosomes, with relative levels decreasing as desmosomes matured.
source: Comparison of relative Dsg2 and Ecad levels contained within the DP railroad tracks demonstrated that Ecad levels were enriched in nascent desmosomes, with relative levels decreasing as desmosomes matured (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structured illumination microscopy data presented in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Compared to Ecad levels in nascent desmosomes, Ecad fluorescence intensity decreased by 50% in mature desmosomes.
source: Compared to Ecad levels in nascent desmosomes, Ecad fluorescence intensity decreased by 50% in mature desmosomes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structured illumination microscopy data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The relative levels of Dsg2 stayed constant at all time points examined.
source: In contrast, the relative levels of Dsg2 stayed constant at all time points examined (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structured illumination microscopy data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Relative levels of Ecad along the entire cell border did not change with time.
source: Importantly, relative levels of Ecad along the entire cell border did not change with time (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by structured illumination microscopy data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prior to desmosome maturation, Ecad is significantly enriched in nascent desmosomes.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that prior to desmosome maturation, Ecad is significantly enriched in nascent desmosomes.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the structured illumination microscopy data.

claim: Trans strand-swap dimer formation can be eliminated by mutating a conserved Trp2 to Ala (W2A).
source: Structural studies show that trans strand-swap dimer formation can be eliminated by mutating a conserved Trp2 to Ala (W2A) (Harrison et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harrison et al., 2010.

claim: Mutating a conserved Lys14 to Glu (K14E) eliminates a key salt-bridge in the X-dimer interface and abolishes X-dimer formation.
source: Similarly, mutating a conserved Lys14 to Glu (K14E) eliminates a key salt-bridge in the X-dimer interface and abolishes X-dimer formation (Harrison et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harrison et al., 2010.

claim: The DM cannot interact homophilically; the binding interaction between opposing DMs (1.4 ± 0.3% in Ca2+ and 1.8 ± 0.3% in EGTA) were comparable to nonspecific binding in Ca2+(1.4 ± 0.1%) and in EGTA (1.1 ± 0.1%).
source: In agreement with previous results (Harrison et al., 2010; Rakshit et al., 2012), we confirmed that the DM cannot interact homophilically; the binding interaction between opposing DMs (1.4 ± 0.3% in Ca2+ and 1.8 ± 0.3% in EGTA) were comparable to nonspecific binding in Ca2+(1.4 ± 0.1%) and in EGTA (1.1 ± 0.1%) (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM force measurements presented in Figure 4.

claim: The DM interacts with Dsg2 in a Ca2+-independent heterophilic fashion; the DM/Dsg2 binding probability in Ca2+ and in EGTA was 6.1 ± 0.5% and 6.9 ± 0.5% respectively.
source: However, when we measured the interactions between the DM on AFM tip and Dsg2 on CS, our data showed that the DM interacts with Dsg2 in a Ca2+-independent heterophilic fashion; while the DM/Dsg2 binding probability in Ca2+ and in EGTA was 6.1 ± 0.5% and 6.9 ± 0.5% respectively, the non-specific interaction in Ca2+ and EGTA was 1.3 ± 0.1% and 1.2 ± 0.1% respectively (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM force measurements presented in Figure 4.

claim: The Ecad/Dsg2 binding interface is different from the previously established interface for Ecad trans dimerization.
source: This demonstrates that the Ecad/Dsg2 binding interface is different from the previously established interface for Ecad trans dimerization.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the AFM force measurements showing that the DM (which cannot form trans dimers) still binds to Dsg2.

claim: Mutating a conserved Leu 175 to Asp (L175D) eliminates Ecad cis dimerization.
source: Since previous studies had shown that mutating a conserved Leu 175 to Asp (L175D) eliminates Ecad cis dimerization (Harrison et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harrison et al., 2011.

claim: The CM forms Ca2+-dependent trans dimers; the binding probabilities in Ca2+ and in EGTA were 4.1 ± 0.5% and 0.8 ± 0.2% respectively.
source: As shown previously (Harrison et al., 2011), our data confirmed that the CM forms Ca2+-dependent trans dimers; the binding probabilities in Ca2+ and in EGTA were 4.1 ± 0.5% and 0.8 ± 0.2% respectively (corresponding nonspecific binding probabilities in Ca2+ and in EGTA were 1.2 ± 0.2% and 1.4 ± 0.2% respectively) (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM force measurements presented in Figure 4.

claim: The interaction of CM (on CS) and Dsg2 (on AFM tip) was comparable to the measured nonspecific binding; binding probabilities of 1.8 ± 0.3% in Ca2+ and 1.5 ± 0.3% in EGTA were similar to measured nonspecific binding levels of 1.2 ± 0.1% in Ca2+ and 1.4 ± 0.1% in EGTA.
source: However, the interaction of CM (on CS) and Dsg2 (on AFM tip) was comparable to the measured nonspecific binding; we measured binding probabilities of 1.8 ± 0.3% in Ca2+ and 1.5 ± 0.3% in EGTA which were similar to measured nonspecific binding levels of 1.2 ± 0.1% in Ca2+ and 1.4 ± 0.1% in EGTA (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM force measurements presented in Figure 4.

claim: Cis homo-dimerization of Ecad requires prior trans dimer formation.
source: Previous simulations (Wu et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2011) and single molecule FRET experiment (Zhang et al., 2009) have shown that cis homo-dimerization of Ecad requires prior trans dimer formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2010, Wu et al., 2011, and Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: The failure to form CM/Dsg2 interactions is not due to the abrogation of Ecad cis dimers.
source: Thus, the failure to form CM/Dsg2 interactions is not due to the abrogation of Ecad cis dimers.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the knowledge that cis dimerization requires prior trans dimerization, which the CM can still perform.

claim: Ecad/Dsg2 dimerization is mediated by L175, which also mediates cis homo-dimerization in Ecad.
source: Taken together, these experiments show that Ecad/Dsg2 dimerization is mediated by L175, which also mediates cis homo-dimerization in Ecad.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the AFM force measurements with the CM mutant.

claim: EKO/PKD keratinocytes are unable to assemble adherens junction (AJs) and desmosomes due to the loss of all classical cadherins.
source: We have previously shown that the EKO/PKD keratinocytes are unable to assemble adherens junction (AJs) and desmosomes due to the loss of all classical cadherins (Michels et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Michels et al., 2009.

claim: Zipper-like patterns of Ecad at intercellular contacts represent early AJs and recruit AJ marker proteins like vinculin.
source: We have previously shown that these zippers represent early AJs and recruit AJ marker proteins like vinculin (Rübsam et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rübsam et al., 2017b.

claim: There was never any enrichment of desmosomal components at intercellular contacts in the absence of AJ zippers.
source: Importantly, we never observed any enrichment of desmosomal components at intercellular contacts in the absence of AJ zippers (Michels et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in the current study and a citation to Michels et al., 2009.

claim: 3 hr after the Ca2+ switch, 93% of Ecad WT was enriched in zipper-like early AJs at sites of intercellular contacts.
source: In agreement with previous results (Vasioukhin et al., 2000), our data showed that 3 hr after the Ca2+ switch, 93% of Ecad WT was enriched in zipper-like early AJs at sites of intercellular contacts.

claim: Only 48% of Ecad-L175D transfected keratinocytes formed AJ zippers, likely due to impaired Ecad cis-dimer formation.
source: In contrast only 48% of Ecad-L175D transfected keratinocytes formed AJ zippers, likely due to impaired Ecad cis-dimer formation (Figure 5A,B) (Harrison et al., 2011).

claim: 66% of Ecad WT zipper contacts were positive for Dsg2 at early time points following the Ca2+ switch.
source: At these early time points following the Ca2+ switch, 66% of these Ecad WT zipper contacts were positive for Dsg2.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Junctional localization of Ecad and Dsg2 increased to 97%, 18 hr after allowing cells to engage in Ca2+-dependent intercellular adhesion.
source: Junctional localization of Ecad and Dsg2 increased to 97%, 18 hr after allowing cells to engage in Ca2+-dependent intercellular adhesion (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 5A and 5C.

claim: Only 39% of Ecad-L175D induced zipper contacts showed Dsg2 recruitment 3 hr after switching to high Ca2+, which increased to 65% at 18 hr.
source: In contrast, only 39% of Ecad-L175D induced zipper contacts showed Dsg2 recruitment 3 hr after switching to high Ca2+ (Figure 5A,C), which increased to 65% at 18 hr
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 5A and 5C.

claim: A direct interaction between Ecad and Dsg2 is required for efficient recruitment of Dsg2 to early intercellular contacts.
source: confirming that a direct interaction between Ecad and Dsg2 is required for efficient recruitment of Dsg2 to early intercellular contacts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the confocal microscopy data showing delayed Dsg2 recruitment in Ecad-L175D transfected cells.

claim: Only 4% of the Ecad-K14E transfected, contacting cells formed zippers at early (3 hr) time-points after switching to high Ca2+ with only 24% showing zippers at late (18 hr) time points.
source: Our data showed that only 4% of the transfected, contacting cells formed zippers at early (3 hr) time-points after switching to high Ca2+ with only 24% of the transfected contacting cells showing zippers at late (18 hr) time points (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1)

claim: K14 is essential for effective AJ formation.
source: confirming that K14 is essential for effective AJ formation (Hong et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by the confocal microscopy data and a citation to Hong et al., 2011.

claim: The few Ecad-K14E AJs that were formed, recruited Dsg2 more efficiently than Ecad-L175D.

claim: Delayed recruitment of Dsg2 to intercellular contacts was not the result of the inability of Ecad-L175D to efficiently form AJs but rather due to absence of direct interaction between Ecad and Dsg2.
source: This result confirmed that delayed recruitment of Dsg2 to intercellular contacts was not the result of the inability of Ecad-L175D to efficiently form AJs but rather due to absence of direct interaction between Ecad and Dsg2.

claim: There is no co-localization of DP and Ecad in the absence of zippers.

claim: Ecad trans interactions precede Ecad/Dsg2 interactions.

claim: DP was not recruited upon transfection of the full-length Ecad-DM (W2A-K14E double mutant) in EKO/PKD keratinocytes, which abolishes Ecad trans adhesion, and thus zipper formation.

claim: Only 28% of Ecad-L175D established intercellular contacts were positive for DP after 3 hr, which increased to 72% after 18 hr.

claim: After 3 hr, 73% of Ecad-K14E mutant contacts were DP positive, despite widespread defects in AJ formation.

claim: Amino acid L175 in Ecad mediates Dsg2 interactions and facilitates early desmosome complex formation in cells.

evidence: This claim is a summary of the confocal microscopy data.

claim: Desmosome assembly is initiated at sites of Ecad trans homodimerization.
source: Our data demonstrates that desmosome assembly is initiated at sites of Ecad trans homodimerization.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ecad and Dsg2 bind via a conserved Leu 175 on the Ecad cis binding interface and form short-lived heterophilic complexes that localize to early desmosomes and efficiently recruit desmosomal proteins to sites of intercellular contact formation.
source: We also show that Ecad and Dsg2 bind via a conserved Leu 175 on the Ecad cis binding interface and form short-lived heterophilic complexes that localize to early desmosomes and efficiently recruit desmosomal proteins to sites of intercellular contact formation.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Biochemical analysis identified Ecad/Dsg and Dsc/Dsg complexes upon removing Ca2+ from the cell culture.
source: Previously, biochemical analysis identified Ecad/Dsg and Dsc/Dsg complexes upon removing Ca2+ from the cell culture (Troyanovsky et al., 1999).

claim: In a physiological setting, L175 on Ecad is important for recruitment of Dsg2 and DP and for efficient desmosome formation.
source: We also demonstrate that in a physiological setting, L175 on Ecad is important for recruitment of Dsg2 and DP and for efficient desmosome formation.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the confocal microscopy data.

claim: It has been suggested that cross-talk between classical and desmosomal cadherins is mediated by plakoglobin, a cytoplasmic signaling protein found in both AJs and desmosomes.
source: It has also been suggested that cross-talk between classical and desmosomal cadherins is mediated by plakoglobin, a cytoplasmic signaling protein found in both AJs and desmosomes (Lewis et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lewis et al., 1997.

claim: A direct physical interaction between Ecad and Dsg2 ectodomains is critical for timely desmosome assembly.
source: While we did not test the role of plakoglobin in desmosome formation, our data indicates that a direct physical interaction between Ecad and Dsg2 ectodomains is critical for timely desmosome assembly.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ecad/Dsg interactions reported here may not be unique to Dsg2 but may occur with other Dsg isoforms as well.
source: It is important to point out that Ecad/Dsg interactions reported here may not be unique to Dsg2 but may occur with other Dsg isoforms as well.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: In keratinocytes, Dsg3 is essential for desmosome assembly.
source: In keratinocytes, Dsg3 is essential for desmosome assembly (Hartlieb et al., 2013; Koch et al., 1997)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hartlieb et al., 2013 and Koch et al., 1997.

claim: A previous fluorescence co-localization and co-immunoprecipitation study reported interactions between Ecad and Dsg3.
source: and a previous fluorescence co-localization and co-immunoprecipitation study reported interactions between Ecad and Dsg3 (Tsang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tsang et al., 2010.

claim: Poor junctional DP enrichment seen at early time-points, which was more impaired than Dsg2 recruitment, may result from the inability of Ecad-L175 to bind Dsg3.
source: Since the EKO/PKD keratinocytes transfected with Ecad-L175D also express Dsg3, it is possible that poor junctional DP enrichment seen at early time-points, which was more impaired than Dsg2 recruitment, may result from the inability of Ecad-L175 to bind Dsg3.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential role of Dsg3.

claim: Desmosome assembly is Ca2+ dependent.
source: Desmosome assembly is Ca2+ dependent and previous models using Dsc2 and Dsg2 propose that desmosomal cadherins assemble in two phases (Burdett and Sullivan, 2002; Lowndes et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burdett and Sullivan, 2002 and Lowndes et al., 2014.

claim: Previous models using Dsc2 and Dsg2 propose that desmosomal cadherins assemble in two phases.
source: Desmosome assembly is Ca2+ dependent and previous models using Dsc2 and Dsg2 propose that desmosomal cadherins assemble in two phases (Burdett and Sullivan, 2002; Lowndes et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burdett and Sullivan, 2002 and Lowndes et al., 2014.

claim: The first phase of assembly is believed to involve the clustering of Dsc into nucleation sites.
source: The first phase of assembly is believed to involve the clustering of Dsc into nucleation sites.
evidence: This claim is based on previous models of desmosome assembly.

claim: Since Dsc2 homo-dimerization is Ca2+ dependent, it follows that desmosome assembly requires Ca2+, even though Dsc2/Dsg2 heterodimers are Ca2+ independent.
source: Since Dsc2 homo-dimerization is Ca2+ dependent (Figure 1E), it follows that desmosome assembly requires Ca2+, even though Dsc2/Dsg2 heterodimers are Ca2+ independent.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the AFM force measurements presented in Figure 1E.

claim: In the second phase of desmosome formation, Dsg2 is recruited to the clustered Dsc2 nucleation sites through an unknown mechanism that is Ca2+ and W2 independent and that relies on heterophilic interactions with other proteins.
source: In the second phase of desmosome formation, Dsg2 is recruited to the clustered Dsc2 nucleation sites through an unknown mechanism that is Ca2+ and W2 independent and that relies on heterophilic interactions with other proteins (Lowndes et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lowndes et al., 2014.

claim: Ecad mediates Ca2+ independent recruitment of Dsg2, and perhaps other Dsgs, to nascent Dsc clusters.
source: Our data suggests that Ecad mediates Ca2+ independent recruitment of Dsg2, and perhaps other Dsgs, to nascent Dsc clusters.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Initial cell-cell contacts subsequently trigger multiple phases of DP recruitment to finally assemble desmosomes.
source: Previous studies have also shown that initial cell-cell contacts subsequently trigger multiple phases of DP recruitment to finally assemble desmosomes (Godsel et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Godsel et al., 2005.

claim: Due to the transient nature of Ecad/Dsg2 interactions, desmosomal proteins recruited to junctions are expected to rapidly segregate from Ecad.
source: Due to the transient nature of Ecad/Dsg2 interactions, desmosomal proteins recruited to junctions are expected to rapidly segregate from Ecad.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the dynamic force spectroscopy measurements showing short-lived Ecad/Dsg2 interactions.

claim: Images of intercellular interfaces are expected to have both overlapping and separate Ecad and desmosomal protein staining patterns.
source: Consequently, images of intercellular interfaces are expected to have both overlapping and separate Ecad and desmosomal protein staining patterns.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the transient nature of Ecad/Dsg2 interactions.

claim: Although Dsg2 and DP show some co-localization at Ecad-positive zippers, significant non-overlapping junctional staining is observed, even within the first 3 hr.
source: In agreement, although Dsg2 and DP show some co-localization at Ecad-positive zippers (Figure 5), significant non-overlapping junctional staining is observed, even within the first 3 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 5.

claim: AJs and desmosomes rapidly segregate into distinct intercellular junctions.
source: This suggests that AJs and desmosomes rapidly segregate into distinct intercellular junctions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of non-overlapping staining patterns.

claim: Ecad-DM directly interact with Dsg2.
source: Although our biophysical experiments demonstrate that Ecad-DM directly interact with Dsg2, imaging of keratinocytes transfected with Ecad-K14E and Ecad-DM show that stable trans Ecad homodimerization is required for DP and Dsg2 recruitment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM force measurements.

claim: Stable trans Ecad homodimerization is required for DP and Dsg2 recruitment.
source: Although our biophysical experiments demonstrate that Ecad-DM directly interact with Dsg2, imaging of keratinocytes transfected with Ecad-K14E and Ecad-DM show that stable trans Ecad homodimerization is required for DP and Dsg2 recruitment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The K14E mutants only localize with Dsg2 or DP when AJ zippers are present.
source: While the K14E mutants are strongly impaired in AJ zipper formation, they only localize with Dsg2 or DP when AJ zippers are present.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data.

claim: Cells expressing Ecad-DM which do not form AJs, also do not recruit DP or Dsg2.
source: Similarly, cells expressing Ecad-DM which do not form AJs, also do not recruit DP or Dsg2.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data.

claim: Ecad trans binding serves as the initial spatial cue for the subsequent recruitment of Dsg2 and consequently for desmosome assembly.
source: These results indicate that Ecad trans binding serves as the initial spatial cue for the subsequent recruitment of Dsg2 and consequently for desmosome assembly.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the confocal microscopy data.

claim: Combined loss of both E-, and Pcad, the two main classical cadherins expressed in keratinocytes, prevents desmosome assembly.
source: These results are thus in line with the observation that combined loss of both E-, and Pcad, the two main classical cadherins expressed in keratinocytes, prevents desmosome assembly (Michels et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Michels et al., 2009.

claim: The cross talk between Ecad trans dimerization and Ecad/Dsg2 binding may be analogous to Ecad cis homodimerization via L175, which occurs only when conformational entropy is reduced by prior Ecad trans binding.
source: Mechanistically, the cross talk between Ecad trans dimerization and Ecad/Dsg2 binding may be analogous to Ecad cis homodimerization via L175, which occurs only when conformational entropy is reduced by prior Ecad trans binding (Wu et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism, supported by citations to Wu et al., 2010 and Wu et al., 2011.

claim: Ecad trans dimers may be needed to bring opposing cells closer together to initiate desmosome formation.
source: Alternatively, Ecad trans dimers may be needed to bring opposing cells closer together to initiate desmosome formation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about an alternative mechanism.

claim: When opposing HeLa cell membranes are brought into close proximity, by the interaction of protein zero neuronal adhesion molecules, desmosomes are formed.
source: In support of this possibility, a previous study has suggested that when opposing HeLa cell membranes are brought into close proximity, by the interaction of protein zero neuronal adhesion molecules, desmosomes are formed (Doyle et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Doyle et al., 1995.

claim: Desmosome assembly is facilitated both by the direct cis interactions of classical cadherins and Dsg and the trans binding of opposing classical cadherins.
source: Based on these previous studies and our new data, we propose a model (Figure 6) whereby desmosome assembly is facilitated both by the direct cis interactions of classical cadherins and Dsg and the trans binding of opposing classical cadherins.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented in the manuscript, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: The trans homodimerization of Ecad from opposing cells serves as a spatial cue to coordinate desmosome assembly.
source: In our model, the trans homodimerization of Ecad from opposing cells serves as a spatial cue to coordinate desmosome assembly.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the data.

claim: Ecad subsequently forms cis dimer complexes with Dsg though the results presented here do not rule out Ecad/Dsg binding in a trans conformation.
source: Ecad subsequently forms cis dimer complexes with Dsg though the results presented here do not rule out Ecad/Dsg binding in a trans conformation.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, with a caveat about alternative conformations.

claim: Once localized within the native desmosome, Dsg dissociates from Ecad and binds to Dsc to form mature desmosomes.
source: Furthermore, the data suggest that once localized within the native desmosome, Dsg dissociates from Ecad and binds to Dsc to form mature desmosomes.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the data.

claim: Since the Dsc2/Dsg2 complex has a longer lifetime than both the Ecad/Dsg2 complex and Dsc2/Dsc2 complex, the Dsg/Dsc interactions likely promote robust cell-cell adhesion and permit the mature desmosome to withstand mechanical force.
source: Since the Dsc2/Dsg2 complex has a longer lifetime than both the Ecad/Dsg2 complex and Dsc2/Dsc2 complex, the Dsg/Dsc interactions likely promote robust cell-cell adhesion and permit the mature desmosome to withstand mechanical force.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the dynamic force spectroscopy measurements.

claim: Under similar experimental conditions, cadherin surface density was previously determined to be 65 ± 18 cadherins per µm2, which corresponds to an average distance of 124 nm between neighboring cadherins.
source: Under similar experimental conditions, cadherin surface density was previously determined to be 65 ± 18 cadherins per µm2, which corresponds to an average distance of 124 nm between neighboring cadherins (Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: Since the separation between neighboring cadherins is an order of magnitude larger than the radius of curvature of the AFM tip, the measured unbinding events correspond to the interaction of only a single cadherin immobilized on the surface and the AFM tip respectively.
source: Since the separation between neighboring cadherins is an order of magnitude larger than the radius of curvature of the AFM tip, the measured unbinding events correspond to the interaction of only a single cadherin immobilized on the surface and the AFM tip respectively.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental setup and previous measurements.

claim: PEG stretching served as a molecular fingerprint for single molecule unbinding since its extension under load has been extensively characterized.
source: PEG stretching served as a molecular fingerprint for single molecule unbinding since its extension under load has been extensively characterized (Oesterhelt et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oesterhelt et al., 1999.

claim: Under conditions where the binding probability was ~6%, Poisson statistics predicts that more than 97% of measured events are from the rupture of single bonds.
source: The cadherins were immobilized on the AFM tip and substrate as described above and the surface density of the protein was empirically adjusted such that the binding probability was ~6%. Under these conditions, Poisson statistics predicts that more than 97% of measured events are from the rupture of single bonds.
evidence: This claim is based on Poisson statistics applied to the experimental conditions.

claim: A K-means clustering algorithm greatly improves the estimation of kinetic parameters in DFS.
source: We have previously shown that a K-means clustering algorithm greatly improves the estimation of kinetic parameters in DFS (Yen and Sivasankar, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yen and Sivasankar, 2018.
